summary:
Goal: tell a farmer how this season's weather will hit yield, and which crop rotation carries less risk.

- Data: NASA POWER daily weather (10 season measures such as rain, soil wetness, dry spells, heat and frost), official yields for 136 regions (US, Spain, Brazil, Poland), and soil from SSURGO/SoilGrids.
- Country functions: one yield function per crop, kept only if it beats chance on regions it never saw. US 14/29 crops, Spain 7/7, Brazil 8/25, Poland 8/13.
- Global functions: the four countries pooled with equal weight. 17 of 22 leave-one-country-out tests pass.
- Unseen tests:
  - Türkiye: 6 of 15 crops pass (76% of crop area).
  - Past disasters: 7 of 9 droughts and 2 of 4 frosts caught, but only ~⅓ and ~⅒ of the loss predicted.
  - Türkiye 2025 frost: missed (wheat −1% predicted vs −14% recorded).
- Deliverable: a rotation explorer on GitHub Pages that compares rotations on yield, water, soil, pests and weather risk, and says how far to trust its warnings. Plus a 7-slide deck in English and in Turkish.
- Limits: region yield isn't field yield; warnings come during the season, not before planting; frost losses are underestimated.
details:
What it does

Field Shift tells a farmer how this season's weather is likely to affect crop yield, and which crop rotation carries less risk. We built one yield function per crop from NASA satellite-based weather and official harvest records. The functions run inside a free web tool, the rotation explorer. A farmer picks a region and sets priorities such as yield, water, soil health, pests and weather risk. The explorer then shows the farmer's current rotation next to up to three alternatives, laid out year by year as field strips, each with a score and an explanation.

How it works

1. For 136 regions in four countries (50 US states, 43 Spanish provinces, 27 Brazilian states and 16 Polish voivodeships), we turned NASA POWER daily data into ten season measures: rain, root-zone wetness, rain minus evaporation, longest dry spell, evaporation demand, mean temperature, growing degree days, heat days, frost days and coldest night.

2. A correlation matrix showed which of these move each crop's yield. MODIS NDVI greenness confirmed the link: in Grand Forks, July greenness tracks spring wheat yield (r = 0.59).

3. Ridge regression turned this into one function per crop. A function was kept only if it predicted regions it had never seen better than chance.

4. We then pooled the four countries, each weighted equally, into one global function per crop. It passed 17 of 22 tests in which a whole country was left out.

5. Finally, we tested on data never used in fitting. Türkiye: 6 of 15 crops passed, covering 76% of the tested crop area. Past disasters: of 16 documented events, 7 of 9 droughts and 2 of 4 frosts were flagged.

Benefits and intended impact

Official yield records exist only in some countries, for some crops and with gaps. NASA weather exists everywhere, so a weather-based function can serve farmers where records are missing. The tool also says how far to trust it: droughts are usually flagged, but only about a third of the loss is predicted, and late frosts are mostly missed. Our 2025 Türkiye frost test showed this. We want farmers and advisors to make rotation decisions with an honest picture of weather risk, not to replace local expertise.

Tools and technologies

- Code: Python (pandas, NumPy, SciPy, matplotlib) for data processing and model fitting; JavaScript for the Google Earth Engine NDVI export and an automated check of the tool; HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the explorer, a single page that works on desktop and phone.

- Hosting and version control: GitHub, with the explorer published through GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages.

- Data: NASA POWER and MODIS NDVI; USDA NASS and SSURGO; Spain's agriculture ministry (MAPA); Brazil's IBGE; Eurostat; ISRIC SoilGrids; FAO-56 crop values.

- Hardware: ordinary laptops; no special hardware.

What makes it creative

- Instead of one model per place, we measure every season as a departure from that place's own normal. This lets Iowa, Andalusia, Mato Grosso and Mazovia teach one shared function per crop.

- The function needs only NASA weather to run, so it can be applied anywhere, including countries it never saw.

- We tested it against real disasters, not only averages.

- The explorer shows its own track record next to each warning.

Factors we considered

- Seasons in Brazil are shifted six months for the southern hemisphere.

- Irrigation hides the effect of weather. This is why maize fails in Spain.

- Records are missing in some years and places.

- Each country is weighted equally so the US doesn't dominate.

- We were honest about limits: regional yield isn't field yield, warnings arrive during the season rather than before planting, and frost losses are underestimated.

- Every number in the tool is labelled as measured, validated or assumed.
